quick_notes.title: Fundamental Rights (Art 12–35)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Equality (14-18). 2. Freedom (19-22). 3. Against Exploitation (23-24). 4. Religion (25-28). 5. Culture/Edu (29-30). 6. Remedies (32).
quick_notes.explanation: Fundamental Rights (FR) are basic human rights guaranteed to all citizens by the Indian Constitution in Articles 12 to 35. The first group, Articles 14 to 18, gives the Right to Equality, meaning everyone is treated equally before the law and no one can be discriminated against. The second group, Articles 19 to 22, gives the Right to Freedom, which includes freedoms like speech, assembly, and movement, along with protections in criminal cases. The third group, Articles 23 and 24, gives the Right against Exploitation, which bans forced labor and child labor in dangerous jobs. The fourth group, Articles 25 to 28, gives the Right to Freedom of Religion, allowing everyone to practice and propagate their religion freely. The fifth group, Articles 29 and 30, gives Cultural and Educational Rights, protecting the language and culture of minorities and their right to establish schools. Finally, Article 32 gives the Right to Constitutional Remedies, which lets a person directly go to the Supreme Court if any of these rights are violated.

quick_notes.title: Important Articles
quick_notes.detail: 14 (Equality before law), 17 (Abolition of Untouchability), 18 (Abolition of Titles), 19 (6 Freedoms), 21 (Life & Liberty), 32 (Writs).
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian Constitution contains important Articles that protect the rights of citizens. Article 14 provides equality before the law, meaning every person must be treated equally by the government. Article 17 abolishes untouchability, which is the unfair practice of treating certain people as inferior based on caste. Article 18 abolishes titles such as royal or noble titles, except for military and academic distinctions. Article 19 grants six freedoms including freedom of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession. Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty, meaning no person can be deprived of their life or freedom except by a fair legal process. Article 32 gives every citizen the right to approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce their fundamental rights by filing a writ, which is a formal written order from the court.

quick_notes.title: Fundamental Duties (Art 51A)
quick_notes.detail: Part IVA. Recommended by Swaran Singh Committee. Added by 42nd Amendment. Total 11 duties (11th added by 86th Amendment).
quick_notes.explanation: Fundamental Duties (Art 51A) are a set of 11 moral and legal obligations that every citizen of India must follow, as listed in Part IVA of the Indian Constitution. This part was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, based on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, and the 11th duty was added later by the 86th Amendment in 2002. Article 51A, which is the only article in Part IVA, says that it shall be the duty of every citizen of India to, among other things, respect the national flag and the national anthem, cherish and follow the noble ideals of the freedom struggle, defend the country, promote harmony, protect the environment, and strive for excellence in all activities. For example, the first duty is to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, and the 11th duty, added in 2002, is for every parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child between the ages of six and fourteen. These duties are not enforceable by courts like Fundamental Rights (FR) are, but they serve as a reminder that citizens have responsibilities alongside their rights.

quick_notes.title: DPSP (Art 36–51)
quick_notes.detail: Part IV. Non-justiciable directives for the State. Art 40 (Panchayats), 44 (Uniform Civil Code), 50 (Separation of Judiciary).
quick_notes.explanation: The Directive Principles of State Policy, or DPSP, are a set of instructions in Part Four of the Indian Constitution, covering Articles 36 to 51, that tell the government what laws and policies it should try to create to make society fair and just. Unlike Fundamental Rights, which citizens can enforce in court, the DPSP are non-justiciable, meaning no one can go to a court to force the government to follow them. For example, Article 40 directs the state to organize village governments called Panchayats, Article 44 says the state should try to make a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens, and Article 50 instructs the state to keep the judiciary separate from the executive branch of government. These principles are like a guidebook for the government to aim for social and economic justice, even though they are not legally binding.

quick_notes.title: Writs (Art 32 & 226)
quick_notes.detail: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto. Used by SC/HC for protection of rights.
quick_notes.explanation: Writs are legal orders issued by courts to enforce fundamental rights. Article 32 of the Indian Constitution gives the Supreme Court (SC) the power to issue five types of writs, and Article 226 gives the same power to each High Court (HC) within its own region. The five writs are habeas corpus, which means “produce the body” and is used to release a person unlawfully detained; mandamus, meaning “we command,” which orders a public official to do their duty; prohibition, which stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction; certiorari, meaning “to be informed,” which quashes an order from a lower court or tribunal; and quo-warranto, meaning “by what authority,” which challenges a person’s right to hold a public office. These writs are the main way courts protect your fundamental rights.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Rights and Duties of a Citizen'. Fundamental Rights (Part III) are the most tested area in SSC Polity. From Right to Equality (Art 14) to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)—every article is a potential question. We also look at 'Fundamental Duties' and 'DPSP'. Do you know which right was called 'Heart and Soul' by Ambedkar? Or how many duties we have? Let's master the citizens' charter today.
